statement: Fixed inventory plus contention equals locking: a phrase the teacher uses very often and asks learners to remember for the rest of their lives.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Fixed inventory plus contention equal to locking.

statement: In the airline check-in demo the fixed inventory is the 120 seats, the contention is 120 people trying to book those 120 seats, and locking is needed to ensure the correctness of the system.
case_study: Airline check-in demo: 120 seats on a trip, 120 users booking concurrently.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Here you see fixed inventory: 120 seats. Contention: 120 people trying to book 120 seats.

statement: In any system in the world with fixed inventory and contention for it, you apply locking; whenever you see fixed inventory and contention, the first thing that should come to mind is locking.
detail: The teacher says locking is needed to ensure correctness 'always'; he repeats the rule after the BookMyShow example ('Fixed inventory, contention, locking').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You imagine any system in the world where there is fixed inventory, there is contention happening for that, you would apply locking to do that.

statement: COVID portal (India, 2020): the government launched a portal to book appointments at hospitals; every hospital had limited slots (say 100) and everyone jumped onto the platform at the exact moment slots opened - fixed inventory with contention.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every hospital had limited seating.

statement: Such a fixed-inventory system (e.g. the COVID portal) would be implemented with locking, though not necessarily pessimistic locking - it may be optimistic locking or atomic instructions; built on a relational database it would look exactly like the airline demo.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: May not be pessimistic, may be optimistic, may be atomic instructions, but the idea was to do that.

statement: IRCTC (the Indian government's train booking system): many people try to book seats on the same train at once; skip lock is how such a system ensures high throughput, and without it the entire throughput would suffer, so the teacher expects their code base to be full of skip locks (and exclusive locks).
detail: This is the teacher's inference about IRCTC's implementation ('Then their code base would be filled with skip locks, right?').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is how you ensure high throughput. If they would not have taken skip lock, entire throughput would be

statement: BookMyShow (movie ticketing): a movie screen has limited seating and everyone tries to book the same seats; with an exclusive lock the one who gets it moves forward while others wait for the transaction to complete and then the next one jumps in.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Then BookMyShow, movie ticketing system. You have limited sitting area in a movie screen

statement: Flash sale is very similar to the fixed-inventory problem; when flash sale is designed later in the course, this pattern will be seen in action and how beautifully flash sale is designed around it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Flash sale is very similar to this. When we discuss flash sale, you'll see this in action.

statement: Locking is not implemented at the disk level at all; it happens at the database engine level, on the CPU side - a mutex simply does not let the waiting transaction move forward.
detail: Answer to a student asking how the OS and disk handle locking given rows are stored at offsets on disk.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's not happening at disk level. Not at all. It's happening at the engine level, CPU side.
flags: unclear: "From a row is stored in some portion of the day."

statement: Mutexes and semaphores (and in some cases monitors) are the only constructs locking can be implemented with; there is no other way apart from these, otherwise you go for atomic instructions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: mutex or semaphores are the only two constructs that you have.

statement: Holding a seat for, say, 10 minutes while the user completes payment is not SQL locking: a database transaction is not used for that; it is a different system, to be discussed with flash sale.
detail: To the idea of keeping a lock for 10 minutes the reply was 'You would never want to do that.'
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: No, it's different. It's not SQL locking. It's not implemented.
flags: check: speaker of 'You would never want to do that' (Teacher?)

statement: Flash sale will be designed in the seventh week (Sunday), where seat holding becomes clear; three concepts needed to build it are covered before that, in weeks three, five and six.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So seventh week, Sunday, because there it would be very clear.

statement: A seat reserved during payment is not locked but kept 'on hold'; 'hold' is the better word to model it, because 'lock' suggests MySQL is blocking the row, which is not what happens.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's on hold. So hold is the better word to do to talk about it, because when you hear lock, MySQL is blocking it.

statement: When the user picks a specific seat (BookMyShow, airline seat choice), you cannot hand them another seat, so you would not use SKIP LOCKED; you would use just the plain SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on that seat.
case_study: Airline check-in demo: 120 seats on a trip, 120 users booking concurrently.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: No, we would not have skip locked. We would have just this.

statement: With a pointed query on a specific seat (e.g. ID = 67) and FOR UPDATE, a waiting transaction re-evaluates for that same seat once the lock is released.
detail: Teacher answered 'Correct.'
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: So for update also, right? It will wait and re-evaluate for that seat, right?

statement: A student suggested that, with a pointed seat query and FOR UPDATE, the waiting transaction would then try to get another seat.
detail: Corrected: it would not, because the SQL query (pinned to that seat's ID) does not allow it to match any other row.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: No, why would it get another seat? Your SQL query does not allow you to do that.

statement: When the pointed seat has already been taken, the losing transaction's query finds no row: MySQL reports that no rows matched.
detail: The student said 'it will fail for error'; the 'Exactly' replies are labelled Teacher? in the transcript.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It would say no row found over here. Basically no rows matched.

statement: Booking a seat the user picked granularly: in a transaction, SELECT that seat FOR UPDATE, then update it; two transactions cannot take the same seat - one succeeds, the other sees no rows found (or waits, then finds no rows match) and the front end shows 'seat's gone'. Everything else stays the same.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: one would succeed, other would see no rows found, or it would wait and then you would find no rows match

statement: A student asked how a FOR SHARE (shared) lock held by a first transaction that then updates the row affects a second transaction reading the same row; the teacher did not answer in detail (it would need a half-hour lock-timeline chart) and asked students to code it out instead.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: if I go into those details, I would have to write, draw that entire chart on how that

statement: To experiment with locks: start MySQL, open two terminals connected to the same server, set autocommit to 0, begin a transaction in each, acquire shared and exclusive locks and watch how the database reacts - one session halts while the other moves.
detail: The teacher says it is very easy to mimic and no code is even needed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: start a MySQL server on two different terminals connected on the same server and then set auto commit or set auto commit to zero.

statement: Doing the two-terminal lock experiment is also where you discover deadlocks: your code fails and a lot of 'funny things' happen.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And it is going to be because that's where you would also discover deadlocks. Your code would fail.

statement: With SKIP LOCKED, if a transaction that took seat 2 fails, seat 2 is not lost: the next transaction that reads (re-evaluates) the query 'trip_id = 1 and user_id is null order by id' matches that row again; a row is never skipped altogether.
case_study: Airline check-in demo: 120 seats on a trip, 120 users booking concurrently.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: It's not that a row would be skipped all together, right?
flags: check: "reused somewhere" may end the student's question - diarization boundary

statement: Rows are not assigned in order (first transaction -> first row, second -> second row); whichever transaction executes (re-evaluates) gets the matching row, including a row released by a failed transaction.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's not that first transaction is getting first row. Second transaction is getting second row. It's not like that.

statement: A student thought the booking query is evaluated only once, at the start, for all waiting transactions.
detail: Corrected: the evaluation is retriggered whenever a blocked transaction gets a signal.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: When a block transaction gets a signal, it's retriggered.

statement: MySQL's source code uses these exact terms (signals and so on), which is why the teacher uses them; it is easy-to-read C/C++ code, though it may feel overwhelming at first.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you go through MySQL's code base, you will find these exact words, which is why I'm using those terms, signals and all.

statement: The teacher built his understanding by reading MySQL's code: he knows exactly how transactions are implemented and why, how they behave, and why locking is not at disk level.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And for me, I built this understanding because I went through the code.

statement: Dedicate one week of your time to going through MySQL source code; you will not regret it, because you get a very deep understanding of database internals.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: dedicate one week of your time into going through MySQL source code. You'll not regret it at all, at all.

statement: Reading database internals has helped the teacher build much more performant systems; he has scaled SQL systems massively because of it and performance tuning.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I've scaled SQL systems massively because of this and performance tuning.

statement: Official documentation always rules: there is a ton of content on mediocre topics but almost none (e.g. YouTube videos) on advanced material, because no one wants to read it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Official documentation always rules.

statement: With SKIP LOCKED (approach five), the booking query is executed about 120 times in total across all threads (one per seat).
detail: The teacher first said 'No, much more than that', then corrected himself: 'Oh no, no, no. Watch out on approach five.'
case_study: Airline check-in demo: 120 seats on a trip, 120 users booking concurrently.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: Watch out on approach five. When you're doing skip lock. Yeah. It will be 120 days

statement: Without SKIP LOCKED (plain FOR UPDATE), worst-case re-evaluations are N(N+1)/2: all waiting transactions re-evaluate, one succeeds, all the rest re-evaluate again, and so on - N + (N-1) + (N-2) + ... = N(N+1)/2.
case_study: Airline check-in demo: 120 seats on a trip, 120 users booking concurrently.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Locking, revaluating, worst cases, N into N plus one by two.

statement: If you drop the SELECT and fire a plain UPDATE instead, the queuing behaviour is decided by the transaction isolation level: whatever the isolation level says, the transaction does.
detail: A student guessed the transactions would get cancelled; the teacher answered 'Isolation level kicks in.'
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: No, isolation level, whatever the isolation level says, that thing, your transaction would do.

statement: A transaction waits (as in approach four) only because it wants to acquire a lock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why was that waiting? Because you wanted to acquire a lock. That's why it was waiting.

statement: FOR UPDATE cannot be used inside an UPDATE: an UPDATE is a one-line command fired directly on the database, and in the teacher's words you have never (explicitly) acquired a lock on any row.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In update, you cannot do for update. In update, you can just pass update this particular row.

statement: Isolation level governs how concurrent plain updates behave: serializable runs them one after another; repeatable read and read committed each have their own particular behaviour.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If it's serializable, it would run one after another.

statement: To take a lock explicitly, run SELECT ... FOR UPDATE first and then the UPDATE.
detail: Student's restatement; the teacher did not explicitly confirm it before the next question.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So is it like, we need to force run select for update first, if you want to take a lock? Select, then update.

statement: There is no explicit unlock: committing the transaction releases all the locks it holds.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why would we unlock? Commit itself means release all the locks.
flags: check: diarization - 'committing the transaction' opens the Teacher's turn at 01:23:46

statement: You never span a database transaction across the payment (e.g. 10 minutes on a BookMyShow seat): the SQL server's throughput would go down drastically.
detail: Raised by a student who doubted FOR UPDATE could work for BookMyShow if the user sits on the payment page for 10 minutes. The teacher notes people say 'lock' only because it is easy to understand.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: You never span your transaction for 10 minutes until the payment is done.
flags: check: STUDENT_2 label may be a different student from the 01:13:43 asker

statement: Seat holding during payment is split into multiple phases: acquire the lock only for that moment, mark the seat as on hold, and commit - not start a transaction, wait for the payment and then commit.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You just acquire the lock for that moment and say that this seat is put on hold.

statement: A student assumed a waiting transaction busy-loops checking the lock (an infinite for loop).
detail: Corrected: thread signaling is used - waiting threads sit in a thread wait queue and are signaled when the lock is released; OS-level constructs come in handy.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: that's why your thread signaling comes in, where you have a thread wait queue and it signals on that.

statement: OS-level fundamentals (thread signaling, disk I/O) were all taught in college; we just never paid attention or knew how they are used. The teacher is a big supporter of formal education.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: big supporter of formal education. Big supporter.

statement: Relational databases do scale; never believe generic statements such as 'relational databases don't scale' - you can do partitioning, sharding, everything on relational databases, you just need to know how.
detail: The teacher hopes the session made students 'fall in love with relational databases' and urges them to explore them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Never believe any generic string, right?

statement: After the break: a distributed key-value store, built in depth on the implementation side - nitty-gritty performance improvements of relational databases (what, when, why and how) with detours into how Redis does things.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: next one are we'll discuss distributed key values, right?

statement: From now on, almost every system covered gets a detailed brainstorming on why decisions are made, rather than the teacher just presenting a solution.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: from now almost for every system that we covered, we'll have a detailed brainstorming rather than me just rambling about solution.

statement: Second-half problem: build a distributed key-value store on top of a relational database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll build a distributed key-value store on relational database.

statement: The word 'distributed' was added to the problem deliberately because folks love it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I've deliberately added the term distributed over here because folks love it.

statement: When asked to design something distributed, do not design it distributed on day zero: first implement a single-node version, then think about distribution; don't jump straight into leader election, Paxos or Raft. Start simple, then scale out.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Start simple and then scale out.

statement: Requirement: the key-value store must be infinitely scalable - by default everything needs to be infinitely scalable.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: By default, everything needs to be infinitely scalable.

statement: Core operations of the key-value store: get a key, put a key, delete a key, and TTL (auto-expiration of keys).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the core operations that we support are get, put, delete and TTL.

statement: This design is not made up: Apache Ignite, one of the most popular key-value stores, is built on top of a relational DB and supports these operations; the teacher went through its source code to understand the system in depth.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Apache Ignite, one of the most popular key-value store built on top of relational DB.

statement: The brainstorming has five parts - storage, optimization of storage, inserts, update and TTL - with small detours into how Redis does some of these things.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: storage, optimization of storage, inserts, update and TTL

statement: Picking the right column type is really important for any database: the key's type determines what kinds of keys the system supports - integer keys only -> an integer column; strings -> you must decide how big a string.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: picking the right type for any database is really important.

statement: As a database designer you need to know how big your key will be, e.g. VARCHAR(16) (the teacher's deliberately small pick), or 24, or larger sizes such as 30 to 60.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: as a database engineer or as a database designer, you need to know how big your key would be.

statement: A student said the value type depends on what is stored: integer for simple values, a bigger string (200-300 words) for JSON objects.
detail: Corrected: you must pick something that works for all; the choice depends not on what is stored but on how the value is accessed.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: No, but then you have to pick something that works for all.

statement: A blob column can store literally anything as the value.
detail: Prompted by students suggesting varchar, then something like blob ('By very large objects').
speaker: teacher

statement: The value's type is determined by how users are allowed to access or query the value (if at all), not by what is stored.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it does not depend on what we are storing, but how we are accessing it.

statement: MongoDB is also a key-value store: it stores JSON against an ID and lets you query on attributes inside the JSON, which needs query capability within the value and therefore a type that supports it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: For example, in MongoDB, MongoDB is also key-value store.

statement: If the value is stored with a suitably typed column, range queries on the value become possible if you want to allow them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: then you can do range queries on that if you want to.

statement: If you need to query inside JSON values, a blob will not work; use a type that supports it, e.g. MySQL's JSON plugin (now natively supported).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: For example, JSON plugin of MySQL, or now it is natively supported.

statement: Design decision for this key-value store: queries are on the key, never the value, so the value is a black box - a blob (or varchar / long text) storing any type of object. That is a good enough schema to start with.
detail: To a student wanting rows of a JSON-supporting type the teacher said 'You can implement it however you want.'
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we are not penetrating within the value to support some functionality, like we are just using values as black box.

verbatim: You don't need created at at all.

speaker: teacher
verbatim: So every key will have, can have a separate TTL.
flags: check: speaker change mid-sentence; "And then we should" may be Student 1

detail: The teacher called this the worst query you can write (see K2-068).
speaker: student (proposal)

flags: unclear: "his worst source your job did not try"

statement: 'DELETE ... WHERE now - created_at >= TTL' is the worst query you can write: it cannot leverage an index because it is a dynamic computation, so every single row must be scanned every single time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You cannot leverage index because this is a dynamic computation.

statement: Store the absolute expiration time: when a key is written with a TTL, store expired_at directly instead of created_at and TTL (keep created_at only if you need it for something else).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: instead of storing created at and TTL, we directly store the expired at time.

statement: Expiry cleanup becomes 'DELETE FROM store WHERE expired_at <= now' with a single index on expired_at - a really efficient query.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Delete store where, basically delete from store where expired at is less than equal to now.

statement: A student proposed soft delete for the delete operation: mark the row as deleted and let a background job delete it later, since a real delete may need internal data structures to be rebalanced.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: We can probably have a soft delete where we just mark it like as deleted.

statement: Soft delete with an is_deleted column: set it to true, and a periodic job runs 'DELETE FROM store WHERE is_deleted = true' - which means two background jobs, one for expired entries and one for soft-deleted ones.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So now you have two background jobs to, one that deletes.

statement: Alternative proposal: piggyback on expired_at - on delete, set expired_at to a negative value that is always smaller than now.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Or you can just maybe like change expired at to some negative value.

statement: Delete becomes an update: 'UPDATE store SET expired_at = -1 WHERE key = K'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So your delete is equal to update.

statement: Using expired_at = -1 for deletes saves a second background job (one job instead of two), which means less CPU, less disk load, fewer reads, and less storage (no extra column).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So like obviously CPU is being used less. And there's less load on the disk also.
flags: check: repeated "Storage" may be crosstalk with Teacher

statement: Reads must also filter out expired keys, because the cleanup job may not have run yet when a key is read.
detail: Student's point; the teacher deferred it: 'we'll come to that when we do get'.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: That once you're reading, just check if the key is expired.
flags: check: speaker of the 01:48:37 lines (unlabelled, likely Student 4)

statement: A single background job 'DELETE FROM store WHERE expired_at < now' matches both expired rows and soft-deleted rows (expired_at negative).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This not only matches the rows that are expired, but also the negative values.

statement: This is an elegant solution: one SQL query absorbs both cases (no separate threads for time-based and soft deletes) and puts minimal load because of the expired_at index.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this is such an elegant solution that solves both the things in one SQL query itself.

statement: A value-type column is only needed if the store supports multiple value types (you could even store serialized YAML and build another Redis on top); with a single homogeneous type such as string, it is not needed.
detail: Prompted by a student suggesting a type column because the value is varchar.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But you can have value type when you're supporting multiple values.

statement: A naive insert passes all three columns: key, value and expired_at.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So key, value and expired at, you would pass all three to do it.

statement: A put triggers an insert: PUT K1 V1 inserts the row; a later PUT K1 V2 fires the same insert again and fails because the key already exists.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It would fire the same insert again and it would fail. Correct? Yep. Because key already exists.

statement: A student proposed handling a repeated put by adding a WHERE clause for expired values.
detail: Redirected: a put is expected to replace the existing value.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: how will, when you do put operation, you expect this to replace this value.

statement: Naive fix: GET every time, then UPDATE if the key exists or INSERT if not - every put becomes a get plus a put, which is expensive because you fetch the key unnecessarily.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So now for every put operation results into a get and a put.

statement: What a put needs: insert if the key does not exist, update if it exists - without explicitly getting the key first.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you'd want to insert if the key does not exist and you want to update if the key exists.

statement: A student proposed handling a repeated put by marking the previous key as expired and creating a new entry with the same key.
detail: Corrected: that still requires getting the key, and the key is the primary key, so two entries with it cannot exist.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: this is your primary key. You cannot have two entries with that.

statement: The devil lies in the details: people just draw boxes and never think about implementation; think about implementation and you see how costly get-then-insert/update is.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The devil lies in the details, right?

statement: A student proposed 'INSERT INTO store VALUES (K1, V1), if it exists do update' - an upsert at the database level; the teacher confirmed this.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Basically we are trying to do an upsert query at the database level.

statement: Upserts are atomic, wrapped in a transaction and a single SQL query: no need to get the row, check whether it exists and then write it in a transaction.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Upserts are atomic, wrapped in transaction and just one SQL query.

statement: Check whether the database you choose supports upsert operations; in Postgres you just replace INSERT with UPSERT to get upsert behaviour.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in case you are using Postgres, you just replace insert with upsert.

statement: Upsert behaviour: PUT K1 V1 (with expiration) stores K1 V1; a later PUT K1 V2 automatically replaces the value with V2 - update if it exists, insert if not.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It would automatically just do replace this V2.

statement: Why upsert is more performant: the database still reads the row, but you avoid the network I/O of bringing data to the API servers - saving a network round trip - and avoid a gigantic transaction wrapped around get+write.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you are not doing that network IO to bring the data to your API servers.

statement: Upsert clauses differ per database: Postgres calls it upsert; MySQL has REPLACE INTO or ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE; pick whatever your database supports.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Postgres calls it upsert, MySQL has a replace into or on duplicate key update, right?

statement: Students should Google these upsert clauses; they will be covered later in this same discussion.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: oh no, today only in this discussion itself, we'll be covering it.

statement: Native upsert statements keep database throughput really high and the load on the database at a bare minimum.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This would keep your database throughput really high when you're using native upsert statements.

statement: Update is straightforward - you directly update - so put and update are the same operation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Update is straightforward. You just go and directly update.

statement: A student proposed handling expiration in the API server: 'SELECT * FROM store WHERE key = k1', then compare now with expired_at and return 'key does not exist'.
detail: Corrected: wasteful - with a 10 MB value you transfer 10 MB to the API only to realise it has expired.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: You are making the 10 MB data transfer to your API eventually to realize that he is expired.

statement: Get query filters expiry in the database: add 'AND expired_at > now' to 'SELECT ... WHERE key = k1'; expired keys are never read out of the database.
detail: The teacher confirmed it and noted what it saves (next item).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So I can also add and expired at, is expired at is greater than now.

statement: That one clause saves heavy network I/O: if values are gigantic you save a ton of it, because you are not even reading the expired value from the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So if your values are gigantic, you are saving a ton of network IO.

statement: Micro decisions matter for database performance: everyone writes inserts and simple selects, but think about the devils in every single line to get performance out of it - have that curiosity.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I just want all of you to have that curiosity.

statement: There is one more performance optimization along similar lines, covered later.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there is one more performance optimization on the similar lines.

speaker: student (question)
verbatim: You anyway have to support Upsert for high throughput.
